posts.title: Agentic AI for Professionals (Part 1)
posts.summary: I used a structured LLM-wiki research process to analyze the architecture of Thomson Reuters CoCounsel. I then translated those findings into a multi-phase implementation plan for a simplified legal research assistant.

claims.text: The research process was iterative and grew in scope over nine passes.
claims.quote: The research started narrow and grew across nine separate research passes over official product pages, press releases, and five YouTube transcripts.

claims.text: CoCounsel uses a fixed catalog of skills rather than an open chat box.
claims.quote: **A fixed, tested catalog of skills — not an open chat box.** CoCounsel includes named skills such as Prepare for a Deposition, Draft Correspondence, Search a Database, Review Documents, Summarize a Document, Extract Contract Data, Contract Policy Compliance, and Timeline.

claims.text: The system is restricted to performing tasks within that specific catalog.
claims.quote: It is restricted to only performing tasks inside that catalog.

claims.text: The system uses a curated, scoped document set rather than the open web.
claims.quote: That constraint turned out to be the right one to build around, not a limitation to route past: a curated, scoped document set someone actually put together by hand, then a single RAG-grounded Q&A skill run on top of it.

claims.text: The development order prioritizes local execution before cloud deployment.
claims.quote: That's not a cost-saving afterthought; it's the explicit build order, and it's also just a more honest way to develop something before paying to run it.

claims.text: The implementation plan is structured as a sequenced, checklist-style guide.
claims.quote: Once the architecture was settled, I asked Claude Code to turn it into a sequenced, checklist-style build plan rather than trying to hold the whole thing in conversation:

claims.text: The first phase of development is complete and the containers started cleanly.
claims.quote: Phase 0 is done — I asked Claude Code to go ahead, and once Docker was actually installed on this machine, `docker compose up --build` pulled the `pgvector/pgvector:pg16` image, built both custom images, and started all three containers cleanly.

posts.outcome: I established a technical roadmap and completed the initial infrastructure for a legal research assistant that mirrors CoCounsel's core design principles.
posts.caveats: The post does not yet cover the RAG core or the specific bugs found during the integration of the LLM layer.

posts.title: Agentic AI for Professionals (Part 2)
posts.summary: I built the core RAG infrastructure for a legal research assistant using a local-first architecture. The system provides a provider-agnostic layer that ensures citations are grounded in retrieved data rather than hallucinated by the model.

claims.text: The system runs entirely locally on a MacBook Air without requiring cloud APIs.
claims.quote: This post is the actual build: Phases 1 through 3 of that plan, all of it running locally on my 32GB M4 MacBook Air through Docker Compose, with Ollama serving both the chat model and the embeddings — no cloud API required to get a working system end to end.

claims.text: The embedding dimension must remain constant to match the specific model used during ingestion.
claims.quote: The `EMBEDDING_DIM` constant matters more than it looks: it's fixed at table-creation time, and it has to match whichever model actually generated the vectors.

claims.text: The system uses a direct pypdf implementation instead of a LangChain wrapper.
claims.quote: It's the same `pypdf` library under the hood as my earlier LangChain RAG project — there I went through LangChain's `PyPDFLoader` wrapper and let `load_and_split()` handle it; here I use `pypdf.PdfReader` directly.

claims.text: The architecture allows switching to a cloud provider via a single environment variable.
claims.quote: Neither needs an API key, a network connection past the first `ollama pull`, or a cent of cloud spend — which is exactly the point of building this layer as swappable rather than hard-coding a single provider: the same code that runs free on my own machine today can point at Anthropic's API with one environment variable change once this is worth paying for, without touching a line of the RAG logic itself.

claims.text: The system ensures citations are accurate because the metadata is pulled from the database rather than generated by the LLM.
claims.quote: The detail I think matters most here: citation *metadata* — case name, medium-neutral citation, page number — is read straight off the retrieved database rows, never generated by the model.

claims.text: The current build does not yet include the frontend interface or the MCP server.
claims.quote: What's still checkbox-unticked in the build plan is the part a screenshot would actually show: Phase 4's React/TypeScript upload-and-chat interface, and Phase 5's MCP server exposing this same skill over the Model Context Protocol — Claude Code is the client I'll reach for first, but any MCP client can call it once it's standing.

posts.outcome: I built a functional RAG core that provides accurate, verifiable citations for legal research. The system is designed to be provider-agnostic, allowing for easy scaling from local models to cloud APIs.
posts.caveats: The current implementation does not yet include the React frontend or the Model Context Protocol server.

posts.title: Agentic AI for Professionals (Part 3)
posts.summary: I built a functional interface and an MCP server for the nsw-legal-research-assistant to expose its core capabilities to both a web frontend and Claude Code. I demonstrated the system by running it through the same workflow used by Thomson Reuters to introduce CoCounsel, featuring grounded Q&A, review, and skill-chaining drafting.

claims.text: The system uses a database selector to query specific legal databases.
claims.quote: That's the reason this app has a database selector.

claims.text: The system prevents hallucinated citations by reading metadata directly from the database.
claims.quote: The citation metadata — case name, page number — is read directly off the retrieved database row, never generated by the model, so *which* excerpt gets cited is the LLM's call, but the citation itself can't be hallucinated.

claims.text: The drafting process uses a stateless approach that forbids the model from introducing new facts.
claims.quote: No new retrieval happens here — the exact answer and citations already on screen get passed straight back to a second LLM call, explicitly forbidden from introducing new facts or citations.

claims.text: The system provides a clear refusal when a user asks to draft from ungrounded information.
claims.quote: That statelessness is also why the guardrail is worth testing honestly rather than cherry-picked: asking it to draft from an answer that hadn't actually established an outcome produced a correct *refusal* instead of a fabricated finding — a clean refusal on ungrounded ground is a stronger trust signal than a draft that always complies.

claims.text: The MCP tools are thin wrappers that call the exact same functions as the REST API.
claims.quote: All three are thin wrappers calling the exact same functions the REST API and the frontend call — same skill, multiple interfaces.

claims.text: The system provides consistent results across different interfaces because they share the same backend functions.
claims.quote: Same shape as the browser — the same mix of grounded and not-found rows across the five documents, the same reused-figures-only drafting behavior — because both interfaces are calling `review_collection()` and `draft_from_answer()` directly, not a second reimplementation of them.

claims.text: The entire stack runs locally using Docker Compose and a FastAPI backend.
claims.quote: Every beat above ran against the full stack live on a Docker Compose setup on the M4 MacBook Air from Part 2 — Postgres/pgvector, the FastAPI backend, and the React frontend, all local, no cloud dependency for any of it:

posts.outcome: I built a multi-interface system that provides grounded legal research and drafting capabilities through both a web UI and an MCP server. The system successfully performs skill-chaining and produces verified citations without relying on cloud services.
posts.caveats: The application is not intended to be a reproduction of CoCounsel at enterprise scale.

posts.title: Agentic AI for Professionals (Part 4)

The feature demonstrates how agentic AI can handle complex tasks like identifying core arguments, fetching relevant authorities, and navigating citation graphs to ground legal reasoning.

claims.text: The Brief Builder is a new feature inspired by Thomson Reuters CoCounsel Legal.
claims.quote: This post is a new feature entirely: **Brief Builder**, inspired by the newly announced Brief Builder feature in Thomson Reuters CoCounsel Legal — take a pleading in, propose candid arguments, develop each one against real authority, and produce a properly formatted motion.

claims.text: The system ensures every key fact is an exact substring of the uploaded document.
claims.quote: Every key fact is verified as an exact substring of the uploaded document before it is ever shown.

claims.text: The app provides one-click leads from a judgment's own citation list when a call is ungrounded.
claims.quote: Along the way, a newer feature gets its first real workout: when a develop call comes back ungrounded, the app now offers one-click leads pulled straight out of an already-fetched judgment's own citation list.

claims.text: The system identifies and presents related cases and legislation from the citation graph without manual input.
claims.quote: Right below that, a feature new to this build: a second section pulls related cases and legislation straight out of the citation graph of documents already sitting in the authority database — no search, nobody typed anything:

claims.text: The app does not fabricate citations to fill gaps in the reasoning.
claims.quote: The behavior worth naming is the same one from every prior beat in this series: the app never fabricates a citation to fill a gap, whether that gap is a single argument with nothing to say or a citation-graph lead that only points *near* the case actually worth following.

claims.text: The system provides a plain-English search result that includes the target case.
claims.quote: Typing the plain-English `defective motor vehicle` instead returns a real, on-topic result set with the target case as the **second** hit:

posts.outcome: I built a Brief Builder that automates the transition from a pleading to a grounded legal motion. The system successfully identifies, develops, and grounds legal arguments using a combination of plain-English search and citation-graph navigation.
posts.caveats: The post uses a fictional case fact pattern where identifying details have been changed.

posts.title: Claude Code (Part 15)
posts.summary: I used Claude Code to identify, program, and debug a TinkerKit LCD Module. The process revealed how the agent can navigate hardware quirks, install missing dependencies, and document its own findings to solve complex integration issues.

claims.text: Claude Code identified the specific serial device and its hardware specifications.
claims.quote: Claude queried the macOS `IOUSB` registry directly and found it: a `/dev/cu.usbmodem1101` serial device enumerating as `USB IO Board`, idVendor `10189` (0x27CD), idProduct `32784` (0x8010) — an ATmega32u4-class board built on the same chip as an Arduino Leonardo or Micro, sitting behind a Genesys Logic USB hub.

claims.text: The agent automatically installed the required toolchain and libraries when it found them missing.
claims.quote: Claude created the project folder, discovered `arduino-cli` was not installed, and worked out the toolchain from scratch: checking serial devices, installing `arduino-cli` via Homebrew, then the `arduino:avr` core and `LiquidCrystal` library.

claims.text: The initial sketch failed to display characters because it used the wrong library and pinout.
claims.quote: My first sketch had used a generic `LiquidCrystal` pinout that never drove the module's real contrast line, so the backlight came on with nothing displayed.

claims.text: Claude discovered that the physical silk-screened label for pin D12 was incorrect.
claims.quote: Claude found a hardware quirk before writing a line of code: the connector silk-screened `D12` is not actually wired to Arduino pin 12 at all — it's wired to pin 11 (PB7).

claims.text: The agent implemented a non-blocking timestamp check to handle the LED timing.
claims.quote: Claude wrote the fix against the real pin, driving it HIGH in the same branch that redraws the LCD each second, then dropping it LOW 100ms later with a non-blocking timestamp check rather than a `delay()` call — so the LED flash and the digit change land in the same instant every time.

claims.text: Claude created a local wiki to store knowledge about the hardware quirks.
claims.quote: Along the way Claude also stood up a small `.llmwiki` in the project — its own notes on the board's real wiring and the sketch's design — so the next session starts from what was actually learned here rather than rediscovering the D12-is-really-D11 quirk from scratch.

posts.outcome: I built a functioning counter that displays on an LCD and blinks an LED. I also established a workflow where the AI documents hardware quirks in a local wiki.
posts.caveats: The post does not show the specific internal logic of the LLM's reasoning process during the research phase.

posts.title: Coding Agents That Never Leave: What Happens to the Roles?
posts.summary: I explore how the roles of business analysts, developers, and support staff change when coding agents maintain solutions instead of just building them. claims.quote: So my guess is: yes, for kinds of fix that are approved in advance, but the ticket does not disappear.

claims.text: An agent cannot decide which business proposal to back or own the assumptions.
claims.quote: What an agent cannot do is decide which proposal the business should back, or own the assumptions inside it.

claims.text: An agent that builds and runs a solution collapses the traditional separation of duties.
claims.quote: An agent that builds and runs a solution collapses it.

claims.text: One agent builds while a different agent or person approves to maintain audit logs.
claims.quote: The likely answer is not to drop the rule, but to split the work: one agent builds, a different agent or a person approves, and the audit log records who did what.

claims.text: Developers will review more than they write while testers write the checks.
claims.quote: Analysts may matter more, developers review more than they write, testers write the checks, and platform engineers run the services the common rules depend on.

posts.outcome: I concluded that if agents stay to maintain what they build, human roles will move toward deciding and checking while the common rules serve as the benchmark.
posts.caveats: Some of these changes have not happened yet and some may not happen.

posts.title: Coding Agents That Never Leave?

claims.text: The primary value of a platform like Dataverse must now be its ability to provide more than just basic common rules.
claims.quote: It is worth paying for only if it gives agents more than the common rules do, at a price that makes sense, in a form they find easy to work with.

claims.text: Technical lock-in may decrease as agents make migration easier, but contractual lock-in remains a risk.
claims.quote: Technical lock-in may weaken as agents make migration cheap; contractual lock-in does not.

claims.text: Agents will happily incur high costs or hit API limits without understanding the underlying contract.

posts.outcome: I concluded that coding agents may make the 'maintenance' argument for low-code platforms weaker unless those platforms offer specific governance advantages that agents cannot replicate on their own.

posts.title: Distillation (Part 1)
posts.summary: I explore the mechanics of hard-label distillation to understand how smaller models can inherit the capabilities of larger models. I conducted a controlled experiment to determine if the quality of a teacher model significantly impacts the performance of a distilled student model.

claims.text: Hard-label distillation uses the same cross-entropy loss as standard next-token prediction.
claims.quote: **Hard-label (response) distillation** is cruder: ask the teacher a question, keep the one answer it wrote, and train the student on that text with ordinary cross-entropy — the same loss every model uses for plain next-token prediction.

claims.text: A model with no prior pretraining cannot learn coherent language from just a few thousand Q&A pairs.
claims.quote: A model with no prior exposure to raw text, trained purely on a few thousand Q&A pairs, learns the *shape* of a good answer — numbered lists, section headers — long before it learns enough English to fill that shape with anything coherent.

claims.text: The student model outperformed the baseline model with a 65.0% win rate in the large-scale test.
claims.quote: Judged on 300 held-out prompts this time (up from 100): **`distilled` won 186, `baseline` won 100, 14 ties** — a **65.0% win rate** excluding ties, with a one-sided binomial test putting this at **p ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁷**.

claims.text: The results show that the distillation technique works regardless of whether the teacher's data was used with permission.
claims.quote: That is exactly what makes the practice usable with a teacher's permission (Phi, licensed OpenAI output) and, allegedly, without it (the accusation against DeepSeek) — the technique itself does not care which.

claims.text: The results remained consistent across both small and large scales of testing.
claims.quote: The mechanism holds up at both scales tested so far.

posts.outcome: I built a system to test the impact of teacher quality on distilled models and concluded that high-quality teacher answers provide a measurable advantage for smaller models.
posts.caveats: The post notes that the accusation against DeepSeek regarding their use of OpenAI's data remains unproven.

posts.title: Distillation (Part 2)
posts.summary: I transformed a pretrained Llama-3.1-8B model into a multi-turn chat model using LoRA on a Mac Studio. I then tested whether a different teacher model, DeepSeek, produced a better student than GPT-3.5.

claims.text: The base model initially failed to know when to stop generating text.
claims.quote: This is the same lesson Part 1's plain pretrained checkpoint taught with single-turn prompts, showing up again in a more specific way: fluency is not the same skill as knowing when to stop.

claims.text: LoRA allows for training on limited hardware by only updating a small percentage of the model parameters.
claims.quote: LoRA leaves the original model's numbers untouched and trains a small set of new ones alongside it instead — 10.5M trainable parameters out of 8.03 billion, 0.131% of the model.

claims.text: The 2048-token limit was determined by testing the actual memory cost of increasing sequence lengths.
claims.quote: 2048 is not an arbitrary round number here; it is the actual, empirically validated ceiling for an 8B model on this machine.

claims.text: The model trained with the DeepSeek teacher outperformed the one trained with GPT-3.5.
claims.quote: **`distilled` won 118, `baseline` won 81, 1 tie** — a **59.3% win rate** excluding ties, one-sided binomial p ≈ 0.0053.

claims.text: The results show that teacher quality, not just scale, is the primary factor in distillation.
claims.quote: This post held scale and architecture fixed and swapped the *teacher* entirely — a different technique for reaching the same underlying claim: teacher quality, not just teacher size or student size, is what response distillation is actually transferring.

claims.text: The model became more repetitive after the LoRA training process.
claims.quote: It is also considerably more repetitive than the single crisp sentence UltraChat's own GPT-3.5 answer gave for the same prompt — a real, honest limitation of roughly one epoch of LoRA on 14,000 examples, not something to hide.

posts.outcome: I built a chat-capable model and concluded that the quality of the teacher model significantly impacts the performance of the distilled student.
posts.caveats: Not every comparison favors the better teacher, as shown by the specific cases where the baseline model performed better.

posts.title: Game Night (Part 1)
posts.summary: I built a suite of multiplayer party games that function as pure static HTML without a backend server. The post explains how I use a peer-to-peer mesh and host-authoritative state to keep all devices in sync.

claims.text: The project uses no database or server process.
claims.quote: There's no database and no server process anywhere in this project.

claims.text: The host browser holds the entire authoritative state of the game.
claims.quote: Every game follows the same pattern: whichever browser creates the room registers a PeerJS peer ID and holds a single global object — I call it `H` — as the entire authoritative state of the game.

claims.text: The system determines a device's role based on the first message it sends.
claims.quote: It waits for the first message to say so:

claims.text: The distinction between a phone and a TV is a simple boolean set by a human.
claims.quote: The only difference between them is one boolean, `isTvHost`, set purely by which button a human tapped — not by screen size, not by user agent, not by anything the browser can actually tell about its own hardware.

claims.text: A peer ID changes every time a browser opens a connection or refreshes.
claims.quote: A PeerJS connection's `peer` id is a fresh random string every time a browser opens a connection — including after a page refresh.

claims.text: The close event does not fire when a user simply closes a browser tab.
claims.quote: The other assumption I had to unlearn: `conn.on('close')` — the event you'd reach for to detect a player leaving — **does not fire when someone just closes the tab.** I measured it directly: a phone closed mid-turn in Plump Trek, watched for 75 seconds, zero close events.

claims.text: A missing heartbeat caused the game to wait 70 seconds for a dropped player.
claims.quote: It costs one timeout the first time it happens per player, rather than every single turn, which is what made a four-player game with one dropped phone unplayable before the fix — the room was paying a 70-second wait every single lap.

posts.outcome: I built a suite of multiplayer games that maintain a synchronized state across a peer-to-peer mesh without a central server. I also developed a robust way to handle silent disconnections in a decentralized environment.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how the system handles network partitions or complex routing issues in a large-scale mesh.

posts.title: Game Night (Part 2)
posts.summary: I explain how WebRTC manages different connection paths like STUN and TURN to connect devices across different networks. I also describe how I use a visual badge to indicate whether a player is using a direct connection or a relay server.

claims.text: TURN is a fallback mechanism for difficult network conditions rather than the standard path.
claims.quote: The important thing I got wrong before I understood this properly: **TURN is the fallback, not the normal path.** Two phones on separate home broadband connections almost always land on 🌐 — STUN alone gets them talking directly.

claims.text: PeerJS defaults to STUN only which can prevent connections on restrictive networks.
claims.quote: PeerJS's default configuration is STUN-only, which is exactly the gap that leaves remote players unable to connect at all when they're behind a restrictive NAT.

claims.text: I use port 443 and TLS to ensure the relay works on restricted corporate or hotel networks.
claims.quote: The `:443` and `turns:` TLS entries matter specifically for devices on HTTPS-only networks (some corporate and hotel wifi block everything except port 443), so at least one of the five candidates gets through whatever firewall is in the way.

claims.text: The relay is the only method that costs money because it routes data through a server.
claims.quote: The relay only kicks in for the genuinely awkward cases, and it's the only one of the three that costs anything, because every byte of game data is doubling back through a server instead of going device-to-device.

claims.text: A badge on the relay icon indicates the connection is passing through a relay server.
claims.quote: A: The connection is going through a relay server rather than a direct path between the two browsers.

claims.text: The test suite forces a relay policy to confirm that the credentials still work.
claims.quote: The end-to-end test suite forces `iceTransportPolicy: 'relay'` to throw away every non-relay candidate and confirm both ends actually light up 📡 against the real Metered servers, which doubles as a check that the credentials still work.

posts.outcome: I built a system that ensures remote players can connect regardless of their network restrictions while providing a visual indicator of the connection path.
posts.caveats: The post does not show the specific internal logic of the PeerJS library, only how I configure it and interpret the results.

posts.title: Game Night (Part 3)
posts.summary: I gave the auctioneer in Going, Going, GONE! a spoken voice using the Web Speech API. I discovered and resolved several distinct reasons why the voice might fail on different devices, including iOS gesture requirements and specific limitations in the Silk browser.

claims.text: iOS Safari requires a user gesture to grant a page permission to speak.
claims.quote: The first real obstacle wasn't a browser gap at all — it was iOS Safari's permission model. iOS grants a page permission to speak **exactly once, and only from inside a user gesture** like a tap.

claims.text: I used a silent, inaudible utterance to consume the one-time gesture allowance on mobile devices.
claims.quote: The fix is to spend a silent, inaudible utterance the moment the voice toggle is tapped — using up that one-gesture allowance immediately, on a piece of speech nobody needs to hear:

claims.text: The Silk browser on Fire TV supports the Web Speech API but reports zero installed voices.
claims.quote: Silk implements one and not the other: `typeof speechSynthesis` is defined, but it reports zero installed voices, so every `speak()` call succeeds as a no-op.

claims.text: I abandoned using pre-recorded word clips because the seams between words were too obvious.
claims.quote: I abandoned it: concatenated single words don't sound like a sentence no matter how good the source voice is, and the better the individual recording, the more obvious the seams between words become.

claims.text: I implemented a system to ensure the auctioneer's mouth moves even when no audio is available.
claims.quote: His mouth still moves even with no voice at all, timed off the same syllable plan a real utterance would have used, so a silent Fire TV doesn't show a character frozen mid-sentence under a caption — `mimeLine()` runs the same animation the real `onstart` handler would have triggered, just on a timer instead of real audio events.

claims.text: I chose to detect capabilities at runtime rather than guessing from a user-agent string.
claims.quote: Two unrelated gaps in the same browser, and the same underlying lesson both times: detect the actual capability at runtime rather than guessing from a user-agent string, and always leave the experience *legible* rather than broken when the answer is no — captions when there's no voice, an older emoji when the newest one is tofu, never a blank box or a character frozen mid-word.

posts.outcome: I built a robust speech system that handles various browser limitations while ensuring the game remains playable and visually consistent for all users.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how the system handles cases where the underlying hardware lacks any audio capabilities.

posts.title: Game Night (Part 4)
posts.summary: I explain how I integrated Google Analytics 4 into a static site to track user engagement and intent. I also describe a small-scale Google Ads experiment to test if paid search can drive new traffic to the games.

claims.text: I use a single shared file to ensure consistent tracking across all games.
claims.quote: A: One place means one implementation, so the events behave the same way in every game and cannot drift apart.

claims.text: I chose not to use the default purchase event because the site cannot verify actual payments.
claims.quote: GA4 ships a default suggested `purchase` Key Event on every property, and I deliberately never touched it.

claims.text: I created a specific redirect page to capture QR code scans that bypass the main page.
claims.quote: The QR scan needed its own tiny redirect page, `bmc.html`, because a phone camera reads a QR code's encoded URL and opens it directly — it never touches the page the image is sitting on, so no `onclick` handler on that page can ever fire for an actual scan, only for someone tapping the rendered image on their own screen.

claims.text: I set a strict cap on ad spending to keep the experiment controlled.
claims.quote: A cap limits the damage, but it does not make the experiment free.

claims.text: I excluded specific keywords like gambling to avoid irrelevant search traffic.
claims.quote: And a short account-level negative-keyword list, because a search for `download`, `apk`, `jobs`, or `buy` has nothing to do with a free browser game — and `casino real money` specifically exists because the card games (Blackjack, Go Fish, I Doubt It) would otherwise pull in real-money-gambling search intent that bounces the instant it lands on a game with no wagering in it at all.

claims.text: I kept the ad budget very low to treat the campaign as a controlled experiment.
claims.quote: A dollar a day with a ten-cent cap per click is about as far from an ongoing ad spend as a live campaign can get — it's closer to a controlled experiment than marketing, and I'm watching GA4's Realtime report for `room_created` events carrying a `google`/`cpc` source before I'd ever consider raising the budget.

posts.outcome: I built a system to measure user engagement and intent on a static site and established a method for testing paid growth.

posts.title: Game Night (Part 5)
posts.summary: I explain how I test a project that lacks a build step, a server, and modules by extracting logic from raw HTML and using transcript-driven tests. I demonstrate how these techniques catch regressions, prevent scope collisions, and verify that the game mechanics are actually fun.

claims.text: The project uses a unique architecture where every game is a single HTML file with inline scripts.
claims.quote: Every game is one self-contained HTML file with an inline `<script>`.

claims.text: I use a specific audit to catch cases where a shared file and a game share a global name.
claims.quote: There's a second kind of audit that's just as sharp, for a completely different failure: **common.js and a game's inline script share one global lexical scope.** A top-level `const`/`let`/`class` name that exists in both is a SyntaxError — not a warning, a SyntaxError — and a SyntaxError takes the *entire* inline script down with it.

claims.text: I use real network connections only when the test must prove the network actually functions as expected.
claims.quote: A: When the thing you are proving depends on the real network, such as whether TURN credentials still work.

claims.text: I use a transcript-driven test to ensure the auction feels fast and impatient rather than just checking constants.
claims.quote: Everything downstream is judged against that transcript, not against a hardcoded number.

claims.text: I use a specific test to ensure the auction remains fast by failing if it takes longer than 32 seconds.
claims.quote: A lot nobody bids on has to be the **fastest** thing in the whole game, not the slowest — it used to take 38 seconds and the test now fails above 32.

claims.text: I use a specific test to ensure the auction feels honest by not shortening the test time.
claims.quote: And the test is honest about its own cost: it takes about three minutes, and the comment says plainly why it isn't shortened — the windows *are* the subject, so speeding it up would test a different, faster, less honest version of the auction than the one anybody actually plays.

posts.outcome: I built a robust testing suite that validates both the technical correctness of the code and the subjective feel of the gameplay.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how the game feels to a human player, only how the transcript-driven tests measure the pacing of the auction.

posts.title: MiniGPT (Part 2)
posts.summary: I explain how a GPT model is grown by training it from random numbers until it learns to predict the next character in a text. I demonstrate that the training process systematically adjusts every parameter to reduce the surprise of the next character.

claims.text: The model starts by producing pure noise because the weights are random.
claims.quote: So what it writes is pure noise.

claims.text: The training process uses a specific number of steps to find good settings for the parameters.
claims.quote: Growing the machine means finding good settings for all of them, and it uses the five steps from Part 1, with one change and one addition:

claims.text: The training code performs the same mathematical operations on every number at every step.
claims.quote: The training code does exactly the same thing on every step, to every number: `loss.backward()` works out every slope by the same rules, and `optimizer.step()` follows them.

claims.text: The larger model uses more blocks and heads to achieve better results.
claims.quote: The stronger model is the same code with bigger numbers: 6 blocks, 6 heads, 384 numbers per letter, and a 256-letter window.

claims.text: The training process uses a learning rate that changes over time to refine the parameters.
claims.quote: **Bigger steps that change over time.** The learning rate starts small and grows over the first 100 steps (*warmup*), so that the random starting numbers are not knocked about too hard, then shrinks gradually along a curve (*cosine decay*) for fine adjustments at the end.

claims.text: The model is kept at its best state to prevent it from becoming a simple memorizer.
claims.quote: Keeping the best copy, not the last one, is what stops the model shipping as a memoriser.

posts.outcome: I built a process to grow a model from random numbers into a functioning system that captures the style of Shakespeare. I also created a follow-along workbook to reproduce these results.

posts.title: MiniGPT (Part 3)
posts.summary: I investigate why large language models use byte-pair encoding instead of reading one character at a time. I compare three different tokenizers to show how larger pieces of text improve performance while increasing the size of the model's internal tables.

claims.text: The letters tokenizer performs poorly when the score is normalized to the actual length of the text.
claims.quote: But its tokens are single bytes, so 0.7214 ÷ 0.693 × 1.00 = **1.040 bits per byte**, the worst of the three.

claims.text: My custom 8,192 piece tokenizer matches the performance of the much larger GPT-2 tokenizer.
claims.quote: **My 8,192 pieces match GPT-2's 50,257.** Bits per byte of 0.697 against 0.700, with under half the numbers (13.9 million against 30.0 million) and in 12.7 minutes against 41.8.

claims.text: The large supply of pieces in the GPT-2 tokenizer did not provide any extra benefit on these stories.
claims.quote: GPT-2's huge supply cost a lot of arithmetic and bought nothing on these stories.

claims.text: Weight tying allows the model to use one table for both token embeddings and the language model head.
claims.quote: The trick is called *weight tying*.

claims.text: The letters tokenizer requires one token for every single character of text.
claims.quote: On the stories I held back for testing, the letters tokeniser needs 1.00 token per *byte* of text (a byte is the computer's unit for one ordinary character, so think of it as one letter), one per letter.

claims.text: BPE builds its pieces by gluing the most common neighboring pair repeatedly.
claims.quote: BPE builds its pieces by gluing the most common neighbouring pair, again and again.

posts.outcome: I built a system that demonstrates how BPE allows models to process larger chunks of text efficiently. I concluded that my 8,192 piece tokenizer achieves the same results as GPT-2 with significantly fewer parameters.
posts.caveats: The study shows that the large supply of pieces in GPT-2 did not provide any benefit on the specific TinyStories dataset.

posts.title: MiniGPT (Part 4)
posts.summary: I rebuild the MiniGPT machine using Apple's MLX library to explore how different engines affect performance on Apple Silicon. I find that while the machine remains the same, the MLX engine provides significant speed and memory advantages through unified memory and compiled training steps.

claims.text: The MLX engine provides a significant speed advantage when the training step is compiled.
claims.quote: With it, MLX is about a quarter faster than itself, and 16% faster than PyTorch.

claims.text: MLX uses less memory than PyTorch for the exact same machine and task.
claims.quote: **MLX uses less memory either way:** 3.7 to 3.9 GB against PyTorch's 4.6 GB, about 15 to 20% less for exactly the same machine.

claims.text: The results from both the PyTorch and MLX versions are nearly identical.
claims.quote: But they should end up in the same place, and they do: after 3,000 steps, the MLX machine scores **0.689 bits per byte** on the test stories, and the PyTorch machine from Part 3 scores **0.697**.

claims.text: MLX avoids memory copying because Apple chips share a single pool of memory.
claims.quote: MLX is built around that, so there is nothing to copy and no `.to(device)` anywhere: the training batch goes straight into an MLX array, and the GPU reads it where it is.

claims.text: Lazy evaluation allows MLX to see the full list of steps before it starts.
claims.quote: That sounds like a delay, but it gives MLX the whole list of steps before it starts, so it can see which ones can be done together, and which ones are never needed at all.

claims.text: The difference in scores between the two engines is roughly the same as the difference caused by random initialization.
claims.quote: That gap is about the size of the luck between two random starts of the same machine: in Part 5, three random starts of one design scored up to 0.007 apart.

posts.outcome: I built a version of MiniGPT in MLX that runs faster and uses less memory than the PyTorch version while producing the same results. I concluded that the engine determines how calculations run, while the machine defines what to calculate.
posts.caveats: The two versions do not start from exactly the same random numbers because the two libraries draw their starting parameters differently.

posts.title: MiniGPT (Part 5)
posts.summary: I investigate four specific architectural changes Meta made to the transformer block for Llama 3.2. I find that rotary position embeddings are the primary driver of performance gains, while other changes like shared keys and values provide efficiency without affecting accuracy.

claims.text: Rotary position embeddings are the primary reason the new block outperforms the 2017 version.
claims.quote: **Turning, RoPE, is the whole difference.** On average, the new block beats the 2017 block by 0.013 bits per byte, about twice the band of luck.

claims.text: Sharing keys and values reduces the number of parameters without hurting performance.
claims.quote: **Sharing keys and values is free.** Full keys and values for every head scored 0.6721, inside the band, while needing 1.2 million more numbers, about a tenth of the machine.

claims.text: The difference between the gated MLP and the standard MLP is not measurable at this scale.
claims.quote: Over three random starts each, the averages are 0.6755 against 0.6768: a gap of 0.001, far inside the band.

claims.text: RMSNorm and SwiGLU provide benefits for speed at scale rather than accuracy at small sizes.
claims.quote: RMSNorm and SwiGLU matter more for speed at scale than for accuracy at this size.

claims.text: The new RoPE method ensures that matches depend only on the distance between tokens.
claims.quote: When a query is matched against a key, what matters is the *difference* between their turns, so the match depends only on how far apart the two tokens are, not on where they are in the text.

claims.text: The follow-along notebook includes the results of my own runs for anyone to see.
claims.quote: It is saved with the outputs from my own run, so you can read every result on GitHub without a Mac.

posts.outcome: I built a suite of models to isolate the effects of modern transformer components. I concluded that RoPE is the most significant change for accuracy, while others primarily optimize for scale.
posts.caveats: The results show that RMSNorm and SwiGLU do not significantly improve accuracy at this specific scale, but their benefits are more relevant for larger models.

posts.title: MiniGPT (Part 6)
posts.summary: I explore the concept of knowledge distillation by training a small MiniGPT to copy the 'wheel of chances' from larger teacher models. I find that the most effective teacher is not necessarily the largest or most capable model, but the one whose internal representations and vocabulary align most closely with the student.

claims.text: Standard training only rewards the model for finding the single correct answer.
claims.quote: In the guessing game, the only thing the machine learns from at each step is the one right answer.

claims.text: Distillation requires the teacher and student to share the exact same vocabulary to compare their wheels.
claims.quote: So the teacher must use exactly the student's tokeniser, its supply of pieces from Part 3.

claims.text: A large model that has not seen the specific data can be a poor teacher for a smaller model.
claims.quote: The third column says why: at 1.5 billion numbers, GPT-2 XL is still *worse* at these stories (0.799) than the 30-million-number student trained on them (0.756).

claims.text: A smaller teacher that is well-suited to the specific task outperformed a much larger, general-purpose teacher.
claims.quote: A teacher who knew the stories beat one 45 times its size that did not.

claims.text: The most helpful teacher is one whose wheels the student can actually copy.
claims.quote: The most helpful teacher was not the best storyteller: it was the one built like the student and trained on the same stories, whose wheels the student could actually copy.

claims.text: Running a teacher model during training increases the memory requirements of the system.
claims.quote: Running a teacher every step costs memory: 5.4 GB grew to 11 to 17 GB.

posts.outcome: I built a distillation pipeline that proves a student learns best from a teacher that shares its architectural constraints and data focus. I concluded that a teacher's utility is limited by the student's ability to replicate the teacher's specific 'wheel of chances'.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how the model performs when the teacher's vocabulary is significantly different from the student's.

posts.title: MiniGPT (Part 7)
posts.summary: I explore why the cost of attention grows quadratically with the length of a row and how a sliding window can mitigate this cost. I demonstrate that while a mask does not save memory, computing in chunks does, and I use a secret-word test to show how far information can travel through stacked blocks.

claims.text: The memory required for attention grows with the square of the row length.
claims.quote: The matches, and the memory to hold them, grow with the *square* of the row.

claims.text: A sliding window limits the number of matches each hidden state makes.
claims.quote: Then each hidden state makes at most 256 matches, and the total grows only *in step with* the row: twice the row, twice the matches.

claims.text: Using a mask to limit attention does not actually reduce the memory cost.
claims.quote: But it saves no memory at all: the machine still works out every match in the full row-by-row grid, and only then throws most of them away.

claims.text: Chunking the row into segments is the method that actually saves memory.
claims.quote: That covers every hidden state's window, and the biggest grid ever built is 256 by 512, however long the row.

claims.text: Full attention required over half the memory of the Mac at 4,096 positions.
claims.quote: **At 4,096, full attention needs 35.5 GB**, more than half the Mac, and 1.9 seconds a step.

claims.text: The chunked window required significantly less memory and time at 4,096 positions.
claims.quote: The chunked window needs 15.1 GB and 0.8 seconds.

claims.text: The 256-position row cannot see information beyond its own window.
claims.quote: **The 256-position row cannot see past its row.** Beyond 256 pieces, the secret has fallen off the front, and it can only guess.

claims.text: Chunked windows allowed the model to process 16,384 positions in 59 GB.
claims.quote: Computing in chunks is what saves memory: 16,384 positions in 59 GB, where full attention stopped at 4,096.

posts.outcome: I built a chunked sliding window implementation that allows the model to handle much longer rows while keeping memory costs manageable. I also proved that information can travel across blocks even when individual windows are small.
posts.caveats: A sliding window only provides the same behavior as full attention if the window is as long as the entire row.

posts.title: Agent Orchestration (Part 1)
posts.summary: I compared three LangChain multi-agent patterns—subagents, skills, and handoffs—to determine which best handles conversational flows requiring clarifying questions. I found that the skills pattern outperformed the others in accuracy and cost while avoiding a specific structural crash caused by nested tool calls.

claims.text: The router pattern is unsuitable for multi-turn conversations because it lacks a checkpointer.
claims.quote: This is the real, structural reason router is confined to single-shot lookups and excluded from the test below — not that it asks or remembers badly, but that both require state it was built without.

claims.text: The skills pattern outperformed both subagents and handoffs in accuracy and cost.
claims.quote: Skills leads on facts and on the judge, and by a wide margin on cost: less than half what subagents spent, and about 70 percent of handoffs' tokens, for a better result than either.

claims.text: The flat pattern is significantly more expensive than other designs because it repeats the entire prompt for every turn.
claims.quote: Flat asked again on the follow-up even though that was not expected, and each `ask_user` interrupt replays the entire ~35,000-token document prompt: its two turns cost 107,280 and 108,209 prompt tokens — seven to seventeen times what skills (14,593 / 4,829), subagents (14,875 / 7,750) or handoffs (14,664 / 4,809) paid for the identical conversation.

claims.text: A specific nesting depth in the subagents pattern caused a tool-call formatting crash.
claims.quote: A tool call an agent makes from inside another agent's own tool call is not just an ordinary reliability risk with extra steps: across this project, one local model family's `ask_user` formatting crash only ever happened at exactly that nesting depth, on subagents, and never once on a top-level `ask_user` call, across flat, skills or handoffs.

claims.text: The judge model provides a high-quality evaluation but is still just one model's opinion.
claims.quote: The judge model is a step up from a keyword check, but it is itself one model's opinion, not ground truth; I found and fixed one case where it hallucinated a full grade for an answer it had never seen.

claims.text: Running all specialists on a single model eliminated the crash in the uniform test.
claims.quote: Running every specialist on one model stopped the crash in every conversation the uniform run covered.

posts.title: Agent Orchestration (Part 2)
posts.summary: I explain the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which allows one AI agent to communicate with another as a peer rather than just a tool. I demonstrate the protocol by running a Python sample that includes agent card discovery, raw JSON-RPC calls, and both streaming and non-streaming requests.

claims.text: A2A is designed for agent-to-agent communication rather than tool integration.
claims.quote: A2A solves the next problem up: connecting one agent to another agent it does not control and did not write.

claims.text: The protocol uses standard technologies like HTTP, JSON-RPC, and SSE.
claims.quote: A2A deliberately reuses existing, boring, well-understood technology rather than inventing anything new: plain HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0 for the request/response shape, and Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming.

claims.text: The Python environment setup required a specific version of Python to support the a2a-sdk.
claims.quote: `uv` downloaded a real CPython 3.12 build on the spot, entirely separate from the system's Python 3.9, and used it to create the virtual environment.

claims.text: The raw curl calls revealed that the SDK requires specific PascalCase method names.
claims.quote: A genuine, real mismatch: this particular SDK version (`a2a-sdk==1.1.0`) registers its JSON-RPC methods under PascalCase names derived from its underlying protobuf definitions — `SendMessage`, not `message/send` — confirmed directly from the SDK's own source:

claims.text: The server requires a specific version header to avoid being rejected.
claims.quote: The fix, found in the SDK's own `constants.py`, is one header:

claims.text: Streaming calls return a series of events for every state transition.
claims.quote: Four separate events, each one a real, individually-delivered Server-Sent Event, matching `agent_executor.py`'s own four steps one for one — the task first `SUBMITTED`, then a `status_update` moving it to `WORKING`, then an `artifact_update` carrying the actual result the moment it exists, and finally a `status_update` moving it to `COMPLETED`.

claims.text: Extended cards allow agents to hide specific skills from unauthenticated users.
claims.quote: Two skills instead of one — `echo_bot_super_mode` only ever appears here, never in the public card fetched at the start of this post, which is the whole point of an extended card: an agent can offer more to a client that proves who it is than to one that has not.

posts.outcome: I successfully demonstrated a functional agent-to-agent exchange using the A2A protocol. I proved that the protocol works for both raw wire calls and high-level SDK implementations.

posts.title: Model Context Protocol (Part 3)
posts.summary: I build a Retrieval-Augmented Generation stack to provide relevant context to a language model. I conclude by exposing the search functionality to Claude Code using the Model Context Protocol.

claims.text: RAG provides context by finding relevant text before the model generates an answer.
claims.quote: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG for short, is the pattern behind most of the useful AI applications being built right now: instead of asking a language model to answer purely from what it happened to be trained on, you find the specific, real, relevant text first, hand that to the model as context, and ask it to answer from that.

claims.text: The search function is shared between the HTTP route and the MCP tool to prevent them from drifting apart.
claims.quote: One function serves both the HTTP route and the MCP tool, so the two cannot drift apart.

claims.text: The MCP tool uses a docstring to describe its purpose to the AI model.
claims.quote: The function's docstring — the triple-quoted string directly below its definition — is not a comment for human readers only; MCP clients, including Claude Code, read it directly and show it to the AI model as the description of what this tool does and when to use it, which is why it is written as a clear, complete sentence rather than a terse label.

claims.text: The -T flag is necessary for Docker to ensure the stdio stream remains clean for MCP.
claims.quote: The `-T` flag on `docker compose exec` disables allocating a pseudo-terminal for the executed command — appropriate for a process like this one that communicates over raw stdio rather than expecting an interactive terminal session, and necessary here because allocating one can interfere with the clean stdio byte stream MCP's protocol depends on.

claims.text: The .mcp.json file must be in the project root for Claude Code to find it.
claims.quote: It needs to sit at the very top, next to `docker-compose.yml`, `backend/`, and `frontend/`, not underneath any of them.

claims.text: The project is built in five verified phases to ensure each component works independently.
claims.quote: Five phases, each verified independently before the next one depended on it: Ollama answering a plain HTTP call with 768 real numbers; Postgres running a real vector similarity query against them; FastAPI gluing the two together behind two small endpoints; React giving it a face; MCP exposing the identical search function to an AI agent, no second implementation required.

posts.outcome: I built a functional RAG stack that provides a search tool for Claude Code. This system allows an AI agent to access specific, relevant data through the Model Context Protocol.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how Claude Code will choose to use the tool or how well it will perform with the results.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 1)
posts.summary: I introduce the Scikit-Learn library and demonstrate how it provides a consistent interface for different machine learning algorithms. I compare linear regression and k-Nearest Neighbors to show how different models can produce similar results while using fundamentally different internal logic.

claims.text: Scikit-Learn provides a consistent API for different models.
claims.quote: In both cases, Scikit-Learn gives the model the same two calls, `fit` and `predict`, so swapping one algorithm for a completely different one changes only two lines.

claims.text: Linear regression calculates a specific intercept and slope to make predictions.
claims.quote: **Linear regression learns two numbers.** It works out the straight line that best fits the 27 countries, directly, in one calculation (least squares): an intercept of 3.749, and a slope of 0.0678, the extra life satisfaction for every extra $1,000 of GDP per capita.

claims.text: k-Nearest Neighbors stores the data instead of calculating a formula.
claims.quote: **k-Nearest Neighbors learns nothing.** Its `fit` just stores the 27 countries.

claims.text: The choice of three neighbors is a hyperparameter rather than a rule.
claims.quote: A: The three is a choice, not a law: the notebook sets `n_neighbors=3`, and I did not tune it.

claims.text: The prediction for Cyprus is 6.33 using the k-Nearest Neighbors model.
claims.quote: *I swapped in k-Nearest Neighbors with k = 3, which predicts 6.33 for Cyprus*

claims.text: Neural networks like MiniGPT use backpropagation to nudge weights.
claims.quote: My MiniGPT model starts from 826,433 random numbers and nudges every one of them thousands of times, using backpropagation to find which way each should move.

posts.outcome: I demonstrated that Scikit-Learn allows for easy experimentation by providing a consistent fit and predict interface. I concluded that while different models may yield similar predictions, their internal learning processes vary significantly.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how to choose the best hyperparameter using cross-validation, which is covered in Part 2.

claims.text: The neural network achieved an accuracy of 87.4% on unseen test images.
claims.quote: My network was right on 87.4% of 10,000 test pictures it had never seen.

claims.text: The network consists of 266,610 numbers that it learns from training images.
claims.quote: It had 266,610 numbers, and it learned all of them from the training pictures.

claims.text: The Keras network achieved a score of 0.535 on the California house prices data.
claims.quote: On the California house prices, Scikit-Learn's simple `MLPRegressor` scored an error of 0.505, and the Keras network 0.535.

claims.text: The training process for the clothing classifier involved 51,570 total nudges.
claims.quote: One pass through the 55,000 training images is 1,719 such steps, and the network makes 30 passes: 51,570 nudges in all.

claims.text: The training of the MiniGPT model uses 826,433 numbers and AdamW optimization.
claims.quote: MiniGPT is the same machine at a different scale: 826,433 numbers, 3,000 steps of 32 snippets of text, AdamW instead of plain gradient descent, and attention layers between the dense ones.

claims.text: The notebook took approximately 14 minutes to run on a Mac Studio.
claims.quote: I ran everything before the exercise solutions, which took about 14 minutes on my Mac Studio, most of it in the three hyperparameter searches, and then looked through the results in JupyterLab.

posts.outcome: I built a clothing classifier that successfully identifies items from the Fashion MNIST dataset. I also demonstrated that the same backpropagation principles used here are the same ones that train large language models.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 11)
posts.summary: I explain why deep neural networks are difficult to train and identify the specific techniques that make them successful. I demonstrate how proper initialization, activation functions, and optimizers keep the gradients stable enough for the network to learn.

claims.text: Deep networks fail because gradients shrink or grow excessively as they pass through many layers.
claims.quote: It fails because the slopes, which backpropagation passes back through every layer, shrink or grow at each layer until the early layers barely learn.

claims.text: The SELU activation function allowed the 100-layer network to reach 82.0% accuracy.
claims.quote: In my run, a bend called SELU (scaled exponential linear unit), with matching starting numbers, took the 100-layer network from 69.9% with ReLU to 82.0%.

claims.text: The AdamW optimizer performed better than plain gradient descent in my tests.
claims.quote: How the nudging is done matters too: the same network scored 83.7% with plain gradient descent and 87.9% with AdamW, a smarter way of choosing each step.

claims.text: Batch normalization allows a network with only two layers to reach 86.7% accuracy.
claims.quote: A different trick, rescaling each layer's inputs during training (*batch normalization*), let a network with only two hidden layers reach 86.7% after two passes.

claims.text: Dropout helps prevent the network from memorizing training images when data is scarce.
claims.quote: Starting from a network that someone else has trained, and switching off a random few neurons during training (*dropout*), help when data is short or a network starts to memorise its training pictures.

claims.text: Monte Carlo dropout provides a measure of how certain the network is about its prediction.
claims.quote: The answers vary, and the spread shows how sure the network is.

posts.outcome: I concluded that while the core backpropagation algorithm remains the same, specific architectural choices like SELU, AdamW, and batch normalization are essential to keep gradients stable in deep networks.
posts.caveats: The post notes that dense layers transfer poorly compared to convolutional layers because they cannot reuse patterns found in different locations.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 12)
posts.summary: I open up the Keras fit() call to show how to write a training loop by hand using TensorFlow. I demonstrate that while manual loops provide full control, the standard fit() method is usually the better choice for most tasks.

claims.text: The manual training loop provides full control but can lead to errors.
claims.quote: Writing the loop by hand gives full control and makes it easy to get something subtly wrong, so the book recommends `fit()` unless the extra control is needed.

claims.text: The Huber loss is less affected by a few very wrong answers than standard regression.
claims.quote: The Huber loss squares small errors but only counts large ones in proportion, so a few odd houses do not pull the whole model towards them.

claims.text: The training loop reduced the average error to about 50,000 dollars on house prices.
claims.quote: In my run, the loop took the average error from 0.66 to 0.50 over five rounds, which is about $50,000 on a house price: about the same as the neural networks in Part 10 on this data.

claims.text: GradientTape finds every slope in one trip backwards to make backpropagation possible.
claims.quote: Nudging each number by hand would need one extra calculation per number; the tape finds every slope in one trip backwards, which is what makes backpropagation possible for a network with millions of numbers.

claims.text: A graphics processor is not faster for small models because the overhead exceeds the benefits.
claims.quote: The network is tiny, and each step does so little work that sending it to the graphics processor costs more than it saves.

claims.text: The training loop in PyTorch and TensorFlow produced the same results for the housing data.
claims.quote: The two runs draw different random batches and start from different random numbers, so they do not match digit for digit, but they tell the same story: the loss falls, and the error settles at about 0.50, around $50,000.

posts.outcome: I built a manual training loop to demonstrate the mechanics of backpropagation and automatic differentiation. I concluded that while custom loops are necessary for specific research needs, fit() is the preferred choice for standard tasks.
posts.caveats: The TensorFlow details are less certain because much of the field has moved to PyTorch.

claims.quote: A: TFRecord files are binary, so they read faster and store images and other structures that do not fit in a CSV row.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 14)

claims.text: The flower network memorized its training data almost perfectly.
claims.quote: And an existing network, trained by someone else on a million pictures, was retrained a little to tell five kinds of flowers apart, reaching 91.8% on pictures that it had not seen, though it had memorised its training pictures almost perfectly (99.9%).

claims.text: The CNN had more parameters than the previous network but learned faster.
claims.quote: But it learned faster, after only 10 passes, and got about 3 percentage points more of the test pictures right.

claims.text: The flower classifier showed a significant gap between training and validation accuracy.
claims.quote: When I trained the flower classifier, the training accuracy reached 99.85% and the validation accuracy only 91.83%.

claims.text: The training process for the flower classifier resulted in overfitting.
claims.quote: That gap is called overfitting: the network had started to remember its 2,752 training pictures instead of learning flowers.

claims.text: The Xception model achieved 91.8% accuracy after a two-step transfer learning process.
claims.quote: Then it unfreezes the network from layer 56 on, and continues for 10 epochs with a step size ten times smaller (0.01): that gave 91.8% by the end.

posts.outcome: I built a flower classifier using transfer learning and a CNN for clothing classification. I concluded that starting from a pre-trained network is a superior way to handle image tasks.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 15)
posts.summary: I explore how to process sequences and forecast daily train ridership using recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks. I compare these models against a naive forecast and a statistical SARIMA model to determine when complex architectures are necessary.

claims.text: A simple forecast provides a necessary baseline to determine if a complex model is worth the effort.
claims.quote: **The lesson:** work out what a simple guess scores before building a model, because it is hard to beat by much, and it tells me whether a clever model is worth having.

claims.text: The best performing model used five inputs including bus counts and the day type.
claims.quote: The 5-input model is the best: besides the rail history, it sees the bus history and the type of the next day, which tells it whether to expect a weekday or a weekend.

claims.text: A single-neuron RNN performed worse than a naive guess because it lacked sufficient memory.
claims.quote: A `SimpleRNN` with a single neuron scored 102,752, worse than doing nothing clever.

claims.text: The SARIMA statistical model performed nearly as well as the RNN on train counts.
claims.quote: A statistical forecasting method called SARIMA, which models weekly patterns directly, scored 32,041, close to the network's 29,979 on the train counts alone.

claims.text: Training a model to predict all future days at once prevents errors from accumulating.
claims.quote: Training it to forecast all 14 days at once avoids that: its error grew from 23,219 for tomorrow to between 32,000 and 38,000 from the fifth day onwards.

claims.text: Backpropagation through time makes long sequences difficult to train due to unstable gradients.
claims.quote: A long run of steps is also why RNNs are hard to train: the slopes can shrink to almost nothing or grow wildly, the problem from Part 11, and why the chapter introduces LSTM and GRU cells and layer normalization.

posts.outcome: I built a system that successfully forecasts train ridership and concluded that simpler models are often sufficient for small forecasting problems.
posts.caveats: The results for LSTM and GRU cells are not a fair comparison because those models only ran for five passes.

claims.quote: The translation results above come from the shortened runs, and the book's are better.
