posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 17)
posts.summary: I explore how networks can squeeze data into compact summaries and reconstruct it as new images. I compare autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models to show how different architectures approach the problem of image generation.

claims.text: The narrow middle of an autoencoder forces the network to learn a compact summary of the input.
claims.quote: The narrow middle is the point: a network that could pass everything through would learn nothing.

claims.text: My first GAN attempt suffered from mode collapse by producing the same shirt shape repeatedly.
claims.quote: In my first run, which I cut to 10 epochs, the plain GAN, built from ordinary layers, produced the same black shirt shape for every one of the 32 random inputs I gave it.

claims.text: Diffusion models are more stable than GANs because they learn a simple, fixed task.
claims.quote: A diffusion model avoids that.

claims.text: The 30 numbers in the middle of an autoencoder can be used for tasks like finding similar items or as a smaller input for a classifier.
claims.quote: They are a compact description of each picture, and they can be used for other jobs: drawing the clothing pictures in 2D so similar items sit together, finding odd pictures that rebuild badly, or giving a classifier a smaller input.

claims.text: A variational autoencoder ensures that random numbers in the middle can produce new, meaningful images.
claims.quote: Afterwards, I can throw away the encoder, draw 10 random numbers, give them to the decoder, and get a new picture.

claims.text: Diffusion models have largely replaced GANs in modern image generation.
claims.quote: A: Diffusion models, with larger networks and text prompts added, are behind much of today's image generation, and they have largely replaced GANs.

posts.outcome: I built several models that generate clothing images and concluded that while GANs are powerful, diffusion models offer more stability for generating high-quality images.
posts.caveats: The notebook uses a small scale of data and networks, so the results do not represent the full scale of modern image generation systems.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 18)
posts.summary: I explore reinforcement learning using the CartPole environment where an agent learns to balance a pole through trial and error. I compare policy gradients and various deep Q-networks to show how agents can learn optimal actions without labeled examples.

claims.text: The policy-gradient agent was more stable and faster to learn than the more advanced DQN variants.
claims.quote: The policy-gradient agent learned fastest and most steadily, which is not what I expected: the DQN variants are meant to be the more advanced methods.

claims.text: The dueling double DQN was the only complex variant that remained stable at the end of the training.
claims.quote: They are very unstable, and only the dueling double DQN, the last and most elaborate, was still near the top at the end.

claims.text: The simple rule-based policy performed poorly compared to the target score.
claims.quote: That is nowhere near the 200 steps the notebook treats as success.

claims.text: I saved the best weights because the training for some models was unstable and the final weights could be worse.
claims.quote: Keeping a copy of the best weights, and restoring it at the end, is worth doing, because the final weights may be much worse than the best ones.

claims.text: The training for the fixed-target agent failed after it reached the maximum score.
claims.quote: The fixed-targets agent reached the top score of 200 steps for a long run, from about episode 360 to 480, and then slid to about 10 steps per game by episode 600, where it was no better than random.

claims.text: The replay buffer prevents the network from forgetting earlier lessons by providing a variety of past steps.
claims.quote: The DQN trains on random batches from it, instead of on the most recent steps, because steps in a row are too alike, and training on them makes the network forget what it learned earlier.

posts.outcome: I built a series of agents that learned to balance a pole, concluding that while policy gradients are steady, advanced DQN methods require specific techniques like replay buffers and target networks to remain stable.
posts.caveats: The animations of the cart moving are not shown in the screenshots because they did not display during the capture process.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 19)
posts.summary: I explore how to move a model from a training script to a production environment where other programs can use it. I demonstrate how to serve models using Docker, optimize them for mobile devices, and distribute the training workload across multiple machines.

claims.text: A saved model contains its own description of inputs and outputs so a server can use it without my specific code.
claims.quote: **The lesson:** a saved model is a folder that describes its own inputs and outputs, so a server can use it without any of my code.

claims.text: The TensorFlow Lite conversion reduced the model size by about 3.6 times.
claims.quote: Converting for a phone with TensorFlow Lite made the same model about 3.6 times smaller, 171,748 bytes to 47,928.

claims.text: The server automatically detects and switches to a new version when a new numbered folder appears.
claims.quote: Each numbered subfolder is a version, and by default the server serves the highest number, so saving `0002` next to `0001` is enough.

claims.text: gRPC is faster than REST because it uses a compact binary format but requires a client-side library.
claims.quote: A: REST is simple: any program that can send text to a web address can use it. gRPC is faster, because it sends numbers in a compact binary form, but it needs a library on the client's side.

claims.text: Data parallelism distributes the batch across devices while model parallelism splits a large model into pieces.
claims.quote: In data parallelism, each device holds a copy of the model, each takes a share of the batch, and the slopes are averaged before every copy makes the same nudge.

claims.text: The training accuracy reached 98.30% on the validation set during the multi-device test.
claims.quote: The weights became `MirroredVariable` objects, special variables that keep copies in step, and the training ran as usual: 10 epochs of about 70 seconds each, ending at 96.35% training accuracy and 98.30% validation accuracy.

posts.outcome: I built a system that serves a model via REST and gRPC and demonstrated how to shrink models for mobile devices. I also showed how to scale training across multiple processors using distribution strategies.
posts.caveats: I did not run the sections involving Google Cloud, high-performance clusters, or NVIDIA GPUs.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 2)
posts.summary: I walk through an end-to-end machine learning project to predict California house prices using the Scikit-Learn library. I demonstrate how to move from raw data to a tested model by implementing a pipeline that includes data preparation, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning.

claims.text: The project uses a fictional scenario where a company needs to estimate house costs.
claims.quote: The book invents a company that wants to estimate what a typical house costs in each California district, so that an investor can decide where to buy.

claims.text: The model's performance on training data is not a reliable indicator of its true quality.
claims.quote: A model's score on the districts it learned from tells me almost nothing, because it can simply remember them.

claims.text: The decision tree achieved an error of zero on its training data but failed on unseen data.
claims.quote: The decision tree's error of 0 on the houses it trained on became 67,153 on houses it had not seen.

claims.text: The random forest was selected as the best model for this specific dataset.
claims.quote: They tried a linear model, a decision tree and a random forest, scored all three on houses held back from training, and kept the best, which was the forest.

claims.text: The training process took approximately six minutes on my hardware.
claims.quote: The whole run took about 6 minutes on my Mac Studio, most of it in the two searches.

claims.text: Median income is the strongest predictor of house price with a correlation of 0.69.
claims.quote: Median income is far ahead at 0.69.

posts.outcome: I built a robust machine learning pipeline that successfully predicts house prices by selecting the best performing model through systematic search and evaluation.
posts.caveats: The problem is based on a fictional scenario because the original dataset already contains the actual prices for every district.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 20)
posts.summary: I reflect on the nineteen chapters of Hands-On Machine Learning to identify what remains relevant and what I would change. I conclude that while most of machine learning relies on the core idea of iterative nudging, training processes are often fragile and require careful execution.

claims.text: A model must be judged on data it has not seen to avoid memorization.
claims.quote: **Judge a model on data it has not seen.** A model can memorise what it learned from and look perfect.

claims.text: A decision tree performed poorly on new data despite perfect training scores.
claims.quote: A decision tree scored an error of $0 on its own training houses, and $67,153 on new ones (Part 2).

claims.text: Small and decisive changes can significantly improve model performance.
claims.quote: **Fixes can be small and decisive.** Telling a review model to ignore padding took it from 50.0% to 87.5% (Part 16).

claims.text: Shortening long training runs can lead to poor results.
claims.quote: In Part 16 and Part 17 I first shortened the longest ones to save time, and the results were poor: a picture-drawing model that made one picture, and another that made dark blurs.

claims.text: The PyTorch and TensorFlow implementations produced the same results.
claims.quote: The two gave the same results.

posts.outcome: I concluded that while the core principles of the field are consistent, specific training choices like run length and batch size are critical for success. I also confirmed that different frameworks can yield identical results for the same logic.
posts.caveats: This post is a survey and includes what was current at the time it was written.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 3)
posts.summary: I explore how to evaluate classification models using the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits. I demonstrate why accuracy can be misleading when a target class is rare and show how precision and recall provide a clearer picture of model performance.

claims.text: A high accuracy rate can hide a poor model when the target class is rare.
claims.quote: **The lesson:** a high percentage of right answers can hide a poor model, when the answer I am looking for is rare.

claims.text: The model found only about 65% of the actual 5s.
claims.quote: **Of the real 5s, how many it found.** For my model, 65.1%.

claims.text: A confusion matrix shows what a model gets wrong in a way that a single percentage cannot.
claims.quote: A count of every kind of right and wrong answer, called a confusion matrix, shows what the model gets wrong, which a single percentage cannot.

claims.text: The SGDClassifier is the first model in this series trained by nudging.
claims.quote: The model here, a `SGDClassifier`, is the first in the series trained by *nudging*: its numbers start at zero and are moved a little, over and over, as I explain below.

claims.text: A stricter threshold increased precision to 90% but dropped recall to 48%.
claims.quote: If I make the model stricter about what it calls a 5, it is right more often when it says 5 (90.0%), but it misses more of them (it found only 48.0%).

claims.text: A linear model can start with all weights at zero because it only has one layer.
claims.quote: A: A linear model has one layer, so starting every weight at zero does no harm.

posts.outcome: I built a 5-detector and concluded that precision and recall are necessary to understand the true performance of a classifier.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how to classify all ten digits at once, which is covered in the later sections of the chapter.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 4)
posts.summary: I explore the differences between the Normal Equation and gradient descent for training linear models. I demonstrate that while both methods can find the same optimal line, gradient descent is the only viable method for complex models like neural networks.

claims.text: The Normal Equation and gradient descent both find the same line for a simple linear model.
claims.quote: Both ended on the same line, with an intercept of 4.215 and a slope of 2.770.

claims.text: Gradient descent is the only way to train models without a direct formula like neural networks.
claims.quote: For a neural network, or my MiniGPT model, there is none, so nudging, repeated many thousands of times, is the only way.

claims.text: The learning rate determines if the model converges, creeps, or jumps out of the valley.
claims.quote: The notebook shows all three cases: too small, and the line creeps towards the answer; about right, and it gets there quickly; too large, and every step overshoots, so the line jumps further and further from the answer.

claims.text: The Normal Equation becomes impractical when the number of features is very large.
claims.quote: At 100,000 features the table alone would hold ten billion numbers, about 80 gigabytes, which will not fit in memory.

claims.text: Gradient descent remains efficient because it does not build a massive table of all features.
claims.quote: Gradient descent never builds that table.

claims.text: The Normal Equation and batch gradient descent both found the best line of 4.215 and 2.770.
claims.quote: The Normal Equation and batch gradient descent both found that best line, 4.215 and 2.770; the stochastic methods finished close to it.

posts.outcome: I concluded that while the Normal Equation is faster for small feature sets, gradient descent is the essential method for large-scale machine learning.
posts.caveats: I do not go into the details of logistic regression or the specific implementation of the notebook screenshots.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 5)
posts.summary: I explain how support vector machines find the widest possible street between two classes to create a robust boundary. I also demonstrate how kernels allow for curved boundaries and show that SVMs can be trained both through direct calculation and gradient descent.

claims.text: The support vector machine selects the boundary with the widest empty strip.
claims.quote: The method in this chapter, the support vector machine (SVM), picks the line with the widest empty strip on either side of it, which the book calls a street.

claims.text: The parameter C manages the trade-off between a wide street and training accuracy.
claims.quote: A setting called `C` decides the trade-off between a wide street and a few flowers on the wrong side of it.

claims.text: Kernels allow for curved boundaries by comparing pairs of flowers directly.
claims.quote: A *kernel* lets an SVM draw a curved boundary without computing any extra curved features, using a shortcut that compares pairs of flowers directly.

claims.text: Gradient descent can approximate the direct solution of an SVM within 0.05.
claims.quote: It lands within about 0.05 of the direct answer.

claims.text: StandardScaler is necessary because SVMs measure street width in the units of the features.
claims.quote: That is why the code puts a `StandardScaler` in front of the SVM, in a pipeline like the one in Part 2, so that every feature is on the same scale.

claims.text: Gradient-boosted trees are usually more accurate for tables of data.
claims.quote: They work well on small or medium datasets with many features, but training gets slow as the number of examples grows, and for tables of data gradient-boosted trees (see Part 7) are usually more accurate.

posts.outcome: I built a linear SVM to identify Iris virginica and demonstrated that the same model can be trained using both direct solvers and gradient descent.
posts.caveats: I do not go into the use of SVMs for predicting numbers in this post.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 6)
posts.summary: I explain how decision trees function as a series of yes-or-no questions to classify data. I demonstrate that while these models are highly interpretable, they require regularization to prevent them from memorizing the training data.

claims.text: The model correctly identified 144 out of 150 flowers.
claims.quote: It got 144 of the 150 flowers right, including all 50 setosas.

claims.text: A decision tree is the easiest model to explain because it functions as a list of questions.
claims.quote: **The lesson:** a decision tree is the easiest model to explain, because it is a list of questions that anyone can follow.

claims.text: The tree's prediction is based on the share of training flowers in the leaf.
claims.quote: A tree's chances are just shares of the training flowers in each leaf.

claims.text: Decision trees do not require feature scaling because they use cut-off values.
claims.quote: Each question compares one measurement with a cut-off, so changing its units just moves the cut-off, and the questions still split the flowers the same way.

claims.text: A tree that memorizes every training flower follows the noise and performs poorly on new data.
claims.quote: A tree that carves out a region for every training flower follows the noise, and does worse on new flowers.

claims.text: The tree grew one best question at a time and never changed a previous question.
claims.quote: It never goes back to change an earlier question.

posts.outcome: I built a decision tree that successfully classified iris flowers and concluded that limiting tree depth is essential to prevent the model from memorizing noise.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how ensembles of trees can improve stability, which is covered in the next chapter.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 7)
posts.summary: I explore ensemble learning and how a group of models can outperform any single individual model. I demonstrate that techniques like bagging, boosting, and stacking combine different models to cancel out individual mistakes.

claims.text: A group of different models can beat every one of its members because their mistakes are different and cancel out.
claims.quote: **The lesson:** a group of different models, each only fairly good, can beat every one of its members, because their mistakes are different and cancel out.

claims.text: The best single model I tried was right on 89.6% of the test points.
claims.quote: The best single model I tried was right on 89.6% of the test points.

claims.text: A model that learns how best to combine the others reached 92.8%.
claims.quote: Three different models voting together were right on 91.2% to 92.0%, and a model that learns how best to combine them reached 92.8%.

claims.text: Soft voting counts a confident model more than an unsure one.
claims.quote: Soft voting counts a confident model more than an unsure one.

claims.text: Boosting cannot be trained in parallel because each new model depends on the mistakes of the ones before it.
claims.quote: A: Each new model is trained on the mistakes of the ones before it, so it cannot start until they have finished.

claims.text: A random forest is a collection of bagged decision trees with extra randomness.
claims.quote: It is bagged decision trees, with extra randomness: each split considers only a random subset of the features, which makes the trees even more different from each other.

posts.outcome: I concluded that ensemble methods like bagging and boosting significantly improve accuracy by combining multiple models. I demonstrated that a crowd of models often outperforms any single model in the group.
posts.caveats: The post does not show how gradient boosting differs from the way my MiniGPT model adjusts numbers.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 8)
posts.summary: I explore dimensionality reduction techniques to compress high-dimensional data while preserving essential information. I find that methods like PCA and t-SNE serve different purposes, such as speeding up training or visualizing data, rather than directly improving model accuracy.

claims.text: PCA keeps the most important directions of variation in an image.
claims.quote: A method called principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions in which the images differ most, and keeps only those.

claims.text: Reducing dimensions to 154 numbers keeps 95% of the variation in the original 784 pixels.
claims.quote: 154 well-chosen numbers keep 95% of the variation in an image's 784.

claims.text: Dimensionality reduction is intended to speed up training or help humans see data, not to improve accuracy.
claims.quote: It is worth doing to speed up training, or to draw the data so a person can see it, but it rarely makes a model more accurate on its own.

claims.text: t-SNE is used to visualize high-dimensional data in 2D because it keeps neighbors together.
claims.quote: Methods for curved data, such as t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding), unroll it instead, so that neighbours stay together. t-SNE lays out many-numbered data in 2D so that I can see it.

claims.text: Random projection does not learn anything because it uses a random table of numbers.
claims.quote: Another method, random projection, learns nothing at all: it multiplies the data by a random table of numbers, and the number of dimensions to keep comes from a formula, not from the data.

claims.text: UMAP has largely replaced t-SNE for creating pictures of data.
claims.quote: A: PCA is, constantly: for making data smaller, removing noise, and drawing a first picture of a dataset. t-SNE is still used to look at data, but never to prepare it for a model, and a newer method called UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) has largely taken its place for pictures.

posts.outcome: I concluded that while dimensionality reduction removes some information, it is a vital tool for making training faster and making complex data visible to humans.
posts.caveats: The post notes that some methods like Isomap and locally linear embedding are mostly of historical interest and are not expected in real projects.

posts.title: Scikit-Learn (Part 9)
posts.summary: I explore unsupervised learning by finding groups in data that lacks labels. I demonstrate how clustering can make a small number of labels much more effective for training a classifier.

claims.text: Using clustering to select labels improved accuracy from 74.8% to 86.4%.
claims.quote: When I used clustering to pick which 50 to label, and shared each label with every image in its cluster, it was right on 86.4%.

claims.text: K-Means requires multiple starts because it can settle on a poor answer due to random initialization.
claims.quote: K-Means places its first centres at random, and can settle on a poor answer.

claims.text: K-Means is best suited for finding round, similar-sized groups.
claims.quote: K-Means works well for round, similar-sized groups, and poorly for other shapes, which is why other methods exist.

claims.text: DBSCAN finds groups of any shape by following dense regions.
claims.quote: DBSCAN follows dense regions and finds groups of any shape; Gaussian mixtures give each point a chance of belonging to each group.

claims.text: In my run, the best of 10 starts reached an inertia of 211.6.
claims.quote: In my run, one random start ended with an inertia of 219.6, and the best of 10 starts reached 211.6.

claims.text: The result of clustering is not a single right answer but a way to find structure.
claims.quote: There are no right answers to learn from, so training means finding structure, and each method finds it in its own way.

posts.outcome: I concluded that even without labels, a model can find structure that allows a few labels to go much further. I built a semi-supervised classifier that performed significantly better by using clusters to spread 50 labels.
posts.caveats: Clustering does not know what the groups mean and the groups do not have to match the classes a person would choose.

posts.title: Spec-Driven AI Tools (Part 1)
posts.summary: I tested the OpenSpec tool by running it through two full cycles to implement Programmer and Statistics modes on a custom calculator. I found that while the tool successfully generated accurate documentation and code, its behavior regarding interactive prompts and internal logic choices varied between runs.

claims.text: The calculator project is separated into logic and DOM layers to ensure it is testable.
claims.quote: The calculation engine (`calculator-logic.js`) is separated from the DOM wiring (`calculator.js`), so it is directly testable: twelve tests cover the four operations, chained entry, decimal input, and division by zero.

claims.text: OpenSpec did not ask any clarifying questions before generating the first set of documents.
claims.quote: OpenSpec did not ask a single clarifying question.

claims.text: The tool made several independent decisions regarding bit width and overflow behavior without asking.
claims.quote: That matters, because the request I gave it left real decisions open, and it made every one of them itself:

claims.text: The tool flagged a specific risk regarding the engine level of button disabling.
claims.quote: It also flagged a risk against itself, unprompted: disabling the operator and base-toggle keys is DOM-layer only (matching Programmer Mode's precedent), so calling `engine.setOperator()` directly while Statistics mode is active would not actually be blocked at the engine level.

claims.text: The second proposal used the first one as a precedent for its own logic.
claims.quote: That is a real, observable consequence of `specs/` already holding one archived capability: the second proposal used the first as precedent instead of deciding from nothing.

claims.text: The tool's behavior for the archive command varied between the two runs despite identical conditions.
claims.quote: Same command, same clean-checks situation, different behavior.

claims.text: The final specifications for both features read as accurate documentation of the calculator's behavior.
claims.quote: `openspec/specs/` now holds two capabilities, `programmer-mode` and `statistics-mode`, from two separately archived changes, each still reading as accurate documentation of what the calculator actually does.

posts.outcome: I concluded that OpenSpec successfully produces accurate documentation and code from delta specs, though it occasionally exhibits inconsistent interaction patterns.
posts.caveats: I did not see the tool attempt to merge a modified requirement without losing an existing scenario because neither proposal touched the same capability twice.

posts.title: Spec-Driven AI Tools (Part 2)
posts.summary: I conducted a comparative analysis of two spec-driven AI development tools, OpenSpec and Spec-Kit, by running them against the same set of requirements. I found that Spec-Kit's constitution-driven workflow caught a math error in its own specification and an integer-truncation bug during the convergence phase.

claims.text: Spec-Kit's constitution produced binding rules even when I provided no input.
claims.quote: With no principle input from me, it read the repo itself — README, `package.json`, file structure — and wrote five actual, binding principles: a Separation of Concerns rule (logic/DOM split), Test-First for calculation logic, No Build Step, Simplicity/YAGNI, and one I did not expect:

claims.text: The two tools produced different technical designs for handling negative numbers.
claims.quote: Same ambiguity, same unstated request, two different real designs.

claims.text: Spec-Kit organized tasks by user story rather than by technical layer.
claims.quote: This is a materially different organization from OpenSpec's by-layer tasks.md (engine, then UI, then tests) — Spec-Kit's structure is explicitly built around the idea that a team could split US1/US2/US3 across people and work them in parallel, values the source article specifically praised OpenSpec for.

claims.text: The plan step in Spec-Kit caught a math error in the specification.
claims.quote: Convergence caught a real integer-truncation bug, and the plan step caught a math error in its own spec.

claims.text: Spec-Kit's implementation included features that OpenSpec's proposal excluded.
claims.quote: `/speckit-implement` built the whole feature unprompted: a `dataSet`/`dataEntryStarted`-based engine extension, `toggleSign`/`addDataPoint`/`removeDataPoint`/`clearDataSet`/`requestSum`/`requestAverage`/`requestStdDev`, and a `stats-panel` UI with a per-entry remove button — the User Story 4 scope OpenSpec's proposal had explicitly excluded.

posts.outcome: I concluded that Spec-Kit's constitution-driven approach provides a more robust governance framework that caught specific technical errors during the development cycle.
posts.caveats: The comparison shows that different tools produce different technical designs for the same requirements, meaning the choice of tool impacts the final implementation.

posts.title: Spec-Driven AI Tools (Part 3)
posts.summary: I evaluated the BMAD tool as part of a series comparing three different spec-driven AI development workflows. I found that BMAD is the only tool that proactively asks for clarification on ambiguities and features a robust three-layer review process that caught several bugs before I saw them.

claims.text: BMAD is the only tool that asks for clarification instead of making silent decisions.
claims.quote: **It is the only tool that actually asked.** Every ambiguity I tracked across this series — bitwise/word-size scope, negative-number representation, sample-vs-population standard deviation — BMAD stopped and asked me directly, as real choices, rather than silently deciding (OpenSpec) or silently deciding with written rationale (Spec-Kit).

claims.text: The three-layer review process caught four real bugs before I saw them.
claims.quote: Its three-layer review found real defects and correctly rejected several false findings.

claims.text: BMAD's review process is more proactive than Spec-Kit's convergence feature.
claims.quote: BMAD's review ran automatically, inside the same build pass, before the result ever reached me.

claims.text: BMAD's run cost approximately 2.6 times more than OpenSpec.
claims.quote: The BMAD run cost about 2.6 times OpenSpec's, even though its spec is the most compact of the three.

claims.text: BMAD's review layer correctly identified and rejected several false findings.
claims.quote: The most interesting line in the whole Review Triage Log, though, is a finding the review layer checked and explicitly **rejected as correct behavior**:

claims.text: BMAD is the most expensive and complex tool to set up and run.
claims.quote: It was the heaviest of the three to set up and run, and the most expensive in my runs.

posts.outcome: I concluded that while BMAD is the most operationally heavy and expensive tool, it provides the highest level of safety by asking for clarification and running a thorough automated review.
posts.caveats: The comparison is based on specific versions of the tools and may change as the software evolves.

posts.title: Spec-Driven AI Tools (Part 4)
posts.summary: I compared three spec-driven AI development tools—OpenSpec, Spec-Kit, and BMAD—by running them against identical tasks and feature requests. I found that while they share a common goal, they differ significantly in their approach to ambiguity, verification, and cost.

claims.text: BMAD is the only tool that proactively asked me for clarification on technical ambiguities.
claims.quote: Read across a row and the pattern holds: every ambiguity got a real answer, every answer was different at least once, and in three cases (negative-number format, bitwise scope, stddev formula) BMAD is the one tool that actually asked me instead of deciding on its own.

claims.text: OpenSpec is the cheapest option because it skips the steps of asking the user and performing post-facto verification.
claims.quote: It is fastest and cheapest largely *because* it skips both things that cost the other two tools time, turns, and money: asking you anything, and checking its own work after the fact.

claims.text: Spec-Kit is the most rigorous and conventional tool because it includes an enforced gate called the Constitution Check.
claims.quote: **Spec-Kit reads as the most conventionally rigorous.** GitHub-backed, the heaviest artifact set of the three (`spec.md`, `plan.md`, `research.md`, `data-model.md`, `contracts/`, `quickstart.md`, `tasks.md`, plus a pre-planning quality checklist), and the only one with a literal enforced gate — the Constitution Check, a pass/fail table checked against every principle before planning can proceed.

claims.text: Spec-Kit has significantly more GitHub stars than OpenSpec.
claims.quote: It shows in adoption too, not just structure: as of today, Spec-Kit sits at **139,453** GitHub stars against OpenSpec's **70,691** — checked directly, not quoted secondhand — roughly double, a ratio an independent comparison found holding steady since at least May 2026 (96k vs 47k then).

claims.text: OpenSpec's cost was the lowest in my tests, while Spec-Kit and BMAD were roughly 2.6 to 2.7 times more expensive.
claims.quote: (Sonnet 5 pricing, standard cache-token multipliers — cache write ≈1.25× input rate, cache read ≈0.1×.) OpenSpec was the clear cheapest in my own runs, and Spec-Kit and BMAD landed close together at roughly 2.6–2.7× OpenSpec's cost.

claims.text: BMAD's standard installation path does not support DeepSeek Harness.
claims.quote: **BMAD's usual install path has no DeepSeek Harness support at all.** The Claude Code plugin method this whole series used (`claude plugin install bmad-method@bmad`) is Claude Code/Codex only.

posts.outcome: I concluded that OpenSpec is best for fast, low-cost changes where the user accepts the risk of no automated verification, while Spec-Kit is the superior choice for rigorous, high-assurance workflows.
posts.caveats: I did not test every tool's integration with every driver agent end-to-end, so some compatibility findings are based on documentation rather than live tests.

topics.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
topics.description: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the accuracy and specificity of large language model responses by providing relevant context from a knowledge base at runtime.
topics.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the accuracy and specificity of large language model responses by providing relevant context from a knowledge base at runtime. This approach ensures that the model relies on retrieved data rather than its own internal memory to generate answers and citations.
idea: RAG provides context by finding relevant text before the model generates an answer.
Retrieval ensures citations are grounded in data rather than hallucinated by the model.
Embedding models convert text into numbers to find passages, while separate models write the final response.
Strict rules and curated document sets prevent the model from providing information from outside the provided context.
Context injection is more efficient than including an entire knowledge base in every prompt.

claims.text: RAG provides context by finding relevant text before the model generates an answer.
claims.quote: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG for short, is the pattern behind most of the useful AI applications being built right now: instead of asking a language model to answer purely from what it happened to be trained on, you find the specific, real, relevant text first, hand that to the model as context, and ask it to answer from that.

claims.text: The system ensures citations are accurate because the metadata is pulled from the database rather than generated by the LLM.
claims.quote: The detail I think matters most here: citation *metadata* — case name, medium-neutral citation, page number — is read straight off the retrieved database rows, never generated by the model.

claims.text: The embedding model is only used to find passages, while a separate model writes the final answer.
claims.quote: The agent uses a separate model to write the answer from the passages that the search returns.

claims.text: The system prevents hallucinated citations by reading metadata directly from the database.
claims.quote: The citation metadata — case name, page number — is read directly off the retrieved database row, never generated by the model, so *which* excerpt gets cited is the LLM's call, but the citation itself can't be hallucinated.

claims.text: The system uses a curated, scoped document set rather than the open web.
claims.quote: That constraint turned out to be the right one to build around, not a limitation to route past: a curated, scoped document set someone actually put together by hand, then a single RAG-grounded Q&A skill run on top of it.

claims.text: The vague agent provided information from outside the documents while the strict agent did not.
claims.quote: The difference showed up on questions the documents do not cover: the vague agent answered 3 of 6 of them with legal information the documents do not directly cover, and the strict agent answered none of them that way.

claims.text: Context injection provides the model with relevant information from a knowledge base.
claims.quote: Context injection is a technique that involves providing GPT-4 with additional relevant information from your knowledge base alongside the user’s query.

claims.text: The system ensures that prompts are written more efficiently.
claims.quote: This technique has two specific benefits: (1) prompts are always more efficiently written, and (2) your data are always up to date.

differences.text: The system moved from a vague approach where the model used internal memory to a strict approach where the model only uses the knowledge base.

quotes.quote: It answered 5 of the 6 outside questions confidently from memory, with figures such as a licence renewal fee, Wisconsin speed limits and a stop sign fine.

The difference showed up on questions the documents do not cover: the vague agent answered 3 of 6 of them with legal information the documents do not directly cover, and the strict agent answered none of them that way.

topics.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented generation is a critical architecture for building reliable applications because it grounds the model in specific, verifiable data. By separating the retrieval of facts from the generation of text, developers can significantly reduce hallucinations and improve accuracy.

topics.title: Rules-first design
topics.description: Using AI to build and maintain a rules base from the law, then running the rules, not the AI, when someone asks: what the Minnesota DWI advisor posts show, and where the approach is weaker than the first post claimed
topics.summary: In a rules-first design, a model helps build a rules base from primary sources, and at question time ordinary code applies the rules. The model's only job is reading the person's words into facts. I tried this for a Minnesota DWI advisor, and two posts report how well it worked and how I tested it.
idea: AI reads the statutes and court decisions and drafts each rule with a quote from the source.
A script checks the quotes, and a person approves the change.
At question time the rules run. A small model turns the person's words into facts, and a check keeps only the facts their own words support.
The answer is assembled from templates, and every citation is checked against the statute text.

claims.text: The pattern, in one sentence.
claims.quote: use AI to build and maintain a rules base for one body of law, and run the rules, not the AI, when someone asks

claims.text: Why it is attractive: speed, cost and traceability.
claims.quote: In this case the answers are cheaper and faster, and each figure traces back to the section of the law it came from.

claims.text: Where the model sits.
claims.quote: At question time only the rules run.

claims.text: A small model is enough, because the job is small.
claims.quote: Because that job is small, the model can be small: qwen2.5:7b, running locally, with no frontier model anywhere.

claims.text: Plain rules already read most messages.
claims.quote: Rules alone, with no model at all, read 73% of 150 fresh messages exactly.

claims.text: Little is left for the model to get wrong.
claims.quote: Everything with a legal consequence is code, so there was little for the model to get wrong.

claims.text: A perfect reader and the real small model scored the same on the 2,000 tests.
claims.quote: With a perfect reader the advisor also passed all 2,000, and the real small model matched it.

claims.text: Search engines do not rank a statute above a blog post; the rules base does.
claims.quote: A search engine ranks pages. It does not rank a statute above a law firm's blog post, and our advisor does.

topics.conclusion: The design makes the answers fast, cheap and checkable, and it moves the risk from the model to the rules and the tests. Anything the rules do not encode, such as an inconsistent story or a commercial licence, is a gap that no model will fill. The tests need to come from a source other than the rules.

topics.title: Running models locally with Ollama
topics.description: I have explored using Ollama to run models locally for various applications, ranging from simple chat interfaces to complex agentic workflows.
topics.summary: I have explored using Ollama to run models locally for various applications, ranging from simple chat interfaces to complex agentic workflows. These experiments show that local models can produce high-quality results and eliminate API costs when I provide sufficient detail and select the right model size for the task.
idea: Local models via Ollama can replace cloud APIs for tasks like game generation and automated coding.
Smaller local models require much more detailed documentation and specific instructions to succeed.
Model size directly impacts performance, where larger models offer better reasoning but require more memory and time.
Local models are reliable for specific, well-defined tasks but may struggle with complex, multi-step instructions without a clear plan.
Local execution provides privacy and cost benefits, especially when the generated output is significantly longer than the input prompt.
